name_en: Ceylon OP / BOP (Leaf and Broken Grades)
origin_region: Sri Lanka · all districts (grades, not places)
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Orthodox black tea sorted by sieve and winnowing into leaf grades (OP1, OP, Pekoe, FBOP, FBOPF Extra Special) and broken grades (BOP, BOP1, BOPF, Fannings, Dust); the grade describes leaf size and shape, never quality.
harvest_season: Year-round; each district has its own quality season.
appearance_dry: From long, wiry black OP1 strands to fine, even BOPF particles.
appearance_liquor: Copper to deep red-brown; the smaller the grade, the darker and faster it brews.
appearance_wet: Whole twisted leaf (OP) or small, even coppery fragments (BOP).
taste_profile: Brisk, bright and clean with citrus and light malt; OP grades are lighter and smoother, BOP grades stronger and more astringent.

brewing.notes: BOP: about three minutes; OP: four to five. Leaf grades re-steep once. Brewing a BOP as long as an OP gives a harsh cup.

vintage_note: Grades are the language of the weekly Colombo auction: every invoice is sold as a factory name plus grade, and retailers often label tea simply 'Ceylon OP' (usually a blend of low-grown leaf) or 'Ceylon BOP' (usually high- and mid-grown) without a district. Look for the Sri Lanka Tea Board's Lion logo (pure Ceylon tea packed in Sri Lanka), the district if given, and a pack date; use within a year.
description:
'Ceylon OP' and 'Ceylon BOP' are the two labels you will see most often on Sri Lankan tea, and they describe the size and shape of the leaf, not where it grew or how good it is. OP, 'Orange Pekoe', is a whole-leaf grade of long, wiry leaf; BOP, 'Broken Orange Pekoe', is the same kind of tea cut into smaller pieces that brew faster and stronger. The word 'orange' has nothing to do with the fruit or the flavour; it is a trade term of uncertain origin that has stuck for well over a century.

Sri Lanka's orthodox factories sort every batch by sieve and winnowing into a ladder of grades: leaf grades such as OP1, OP, Pekoe, FBOP and FBOPF Extra Special at the top, broken grades such as BOP, BOP1 and BOPF below, and fannings and dust at the bottom for tea bags. High-grown districts tend to make broken grades, low-grown districts leaf grades, and the Colombo auction sells every invoice as factory name plus grade.

OP grades brew a lighter, smoother, more aromatic cup and need four to five minutes; BOP grades brew darker, brisker and more astringent in about three. Both are clean, bright, citrusy and lightly malty when the tea is good, and both take milk. The common mistake is brewing a BOP as long as an OP and getting a harsh cup.

When buying, look for the Sri Lanka Tea Board's Lion logo (pure Ceylon tea packed in Sri Lanka), a district if the packer names one, and a pack date; tea labelled just 'Ceylon OP' is usually a blend of low-grown leaf, and 'Ceylon BOP' a blend of high- and mid-grown. Use it within a year.

Once you know the grades, the same codes will make sense on Indian, African and Indonesian teas too.
